text:
Within the waters below the Ross Ice Shelf there is the possibility of the existence of a unique group of organisms. The extremely cold marine environment, the lack of light, and the relative isolation from the open sea may combine to produce an environment occupied by highly specialized organisms. Study of this community will be of great value to the understanding of the life processes occurring in a cold dark environment.
Little is known about the possible interchange of waters and organisms from the open Ross Sea to the waters beneath the Ross Ice Shelf. Concurrent observations in the Ross Sea close to the Barrier and through the RISP access hole(s) should provide some understanding of this interchange if it does occur.
The sub-sea sediments should contain significant portions of the Antarctic geologic record that are not present in the known continental deposits. This stratigraphic record will allow some understanding of the fluctuations of the ice shelf and the movement of the grounding line. An analysis of the rates of sedimentation and types of sediments is pertinent not only to the Antarctic but to other areas, particularly in the northern hemisphere, where large ice shelves must have existed during the Pleistocene.
